svg.title: P015 · Product count for every category
svg.desc: One row per category, including categories with zero products. Two categories become three joined rows. Snacks repeats for products 10 and 11. Toys survives with NULL in both Products columns. Snacks reads product IDs 10 and 11 → 2. Toys reads NULL → 0. Counting its whole joined row would give 1. Sort by the computed count: Toys has 0, then Snacks has 2. Category ID breaks a tie. First · FROM Category. The requested population is every category. Starting here gives Toys a row before looking for any products. Second · LEFT JOIN Products. Attach products through the category ID already on the left. Snacks matches two products. The left join also retains Toys with a NULL product ID, which counts as zero products.
svg.text: One row per category, including categories with zero products.
Toys has no products. What would COUNT(*) return for its joined row?
A triangle marks an example to follow. Shaded columns show what to read. Double underlines mark the matching keys. SQL excerpts use … for
Which table gives every category a place?

g.text: The requested population is every category. Starting here gives Toys a row before looking for any products.
Attach products through the category ID already on the left. Snacks matches two products. The left join also retains
Toys with a NULL product ID, which counts as zero products.

svg.text: Two categories become three joined rows. Snacks repeats for products 10 and 11. Toys survives with NULL in both
Category LEFT JOIN Products ON Category.CategoryID = Products.CategoryID
Which column gives Toys a count of zero?
Snacks reads product IDs 10 and 11 → 2. Toys reads NULL → 0. Counting its whole joined row would give 1.
Why does Toys appear before Snacks?
Sort by the computed count: Toys has 0, then Snacks has 2. Category ID breaks a tie.
